# Hardware and Computational Acceleration

Also called: Hardware Acceleration, Computational Optimization, GPU Acceleration for 3DGS

## Overview
Hardware and Computational Acceleration encompasses methods that optimize the rendering and training pipelines of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to overcome memory bandwidth limits, compute bottlenecks, and single-GPU memory constraints. It addresses the problem where the high memory footprint of Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) and the iterative nature of alpha blending exceed the capacity of consumer-grade hardware or limit real-time performance. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the explicit mapping of hardware-specific constraints (e.g., Tensor Core utilization, CPU-GPU transfer latency, cache locality) to algorithmic modifications, such as attribute-wise offloading, GEMM-compatible blending, and view-aware sharding, rather than relying solely on generic compression or sorting optimizations.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by the parent article [Rendering Implementation and Acceleration](21069-rendering-implementation-and-acceleration.md). The core rendering operation involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration strategies generally rely on the following shared mechanisms:

1.  **Tiling:** Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly $16 \times 16$ pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses [S2, unofficial][S4].
2.  **Sorting:** Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending [S2, unofficial][S4].
3.  **Culling:** Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead [S2, unofficial].
4.  **Memory Hierarchy Management:** Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement [S4][S5, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [RoofGS](9830-roofgs.md)
RoofGS is an end-to-end acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rendering pipeline based on stage-specific hardware bottlenecks identified via the Roofline model. It addresses the uncoordinated optimization problem where different stages are constrained by different resources: bandwidth-limited front-end stages prioritize reducing global memory traffic, while compute-intensive rasterization stages prioritize lower instruction cost and increased instruction-level parallelism (ILP). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly mapping memory-centric strategies (compression, fusion) to bandwidth-bound phases and compute-centric strategies (ILP, fast math) to arithmetic-bound phases. See [RoofGS](9830-roofgs.md) for implementation details.

### [Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting](9991-tile-based-comparison-free-sorting.md)
Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting restricts the depth sorting of 3D Gaussian primitives to individual image tiles to avoid global synchronization, reduce hardware complexity, and achieve fixed latency per output. Unlike full-scene sorting methods that incur high memory overhead and variable latency due to global resorting, this method ensures deterministic, fixed per-output latency by matching the front-to-back alpha-blending requirement locally. It is specifically designed for hardware accelerators where predictable scheduling and low power consumption are critical, such as in AR/VR applications. See [Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting](9991-tile-based-comparison-free-sorting.md) for implementation details.

### [Distributed Training and Sharding](15108-distributed-training-and-sharding.md)
Distributed Training and Sharding refers to the family of methods that partition the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and rendering pipeline across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory limits and accelerate city-scale or high-resolution reconstruction. It solves the problem where the number of Gaussian primitives or the resolution of the scene exceeds the VRAM capacity of a single device. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the specific strategy for distributing the global state (Gaussians) and the workload (pixels/views): [BlitzGS](15088-blitzgs.md) uses index-parity sharding to avoid spatial redundancy; [Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting](16979-distributed-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) focuses on scientific volume data with global gradient synchronization; [Distributed Batched Rendering Loop](18495-distributed-batched-rendering-loop.md) and [Grendel](19770-grendel.md) use dynamic, view-aware all-to-all communication to balance pixel-wise loads; and [Online Image Rendering Placement](19195-online-image-rendering-placement.md) optimizes patch assignment via Integer Linear Programming heuristics. See [Distributed Training and Sharding](15108-distributed-training-and-sharding.md) for implementation details.

### [Cache-based Lazy Memory Management](17592-cache-based-lazy-memory-management.md)
Cache-based Lazy Memory Management (CLM) is a memory offloading strategy that enables the training of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by keeping the majority of Gaussian primitives in CPU memory and loading only the subset accessed by the current training view. It distinguishes itself from naive offloading approaches (like Zero-Offload) by exploiting the inherent sparsity of 3DGS memory access patterns, using ahead-of-time view-Gaussian mapping, caching overlapping primitives between views, and scheduling iterations to maximize spatial locality, thereby overlapping communication with computation to hide CPU-GPU transfer overheads. See [Cache-based Lazy Memory Management](17592-cache-based-lazy-memory-management.md) for implementation details.

### [Cache-Less Memory (CLM)](17594-cache-less-memory-clm.md)
Cache-Less Memory (CLM) is a system design that enables the training and rendering of large or highly detailed 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by offloading Gaussian parameters and optimizer computation to the CPU. It solves the problem of GPU memory exhaustion in large-scale scenes by leveraging sparsity and spatial locality to minimize GPU-CPU communication overhead. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex multi-GPU sharding or SSD-based tiering, CLM focuses on algorithmic optimizations like attribute-wise offloading, microbatch pipelining, and precise caching to hide latency and reduce active memory footprint. See [Cache-Less Memory (CLM)](17594-cache-less-memory-clm.md) for implementation details.

## Background
The acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a critical research area following the introduction of the original 3DGS method, which demonstrated high-quality novel view synthesis but suffered from high memory consumption and computational cost during training and rendering. Early acceleration efforts focused on software-level optimizations such as compression and efficient sorting algorithms. As the field expanded to include dynamic scenes, large-scale environments, and mobile deployment, hardware-specific optimizations emerged. The Roofline model has been applied to identify bottlenecks in the 3DGS pipeline, leading to methods like RoofGS that separate memory-bound and compute-bound optimizations [S1, unofficial]. Concurrently, the need for training on consumer hardware led to memory management strategies like CLM, which offload optimizer states and non-critical attributes to the CPU [S1, unofficial][S5, unofficial]. The utilization of modern GPU features, such as Tensor Cores, has also driven the development of GEMM-GS, which reformulates the blending process to leverage matrix multiplication units [S4]. Mobile deployment requirements have further spurred sorting-free methods like Mobile-GS, which trade exact sorting for view-dependent weighting to reduce latency [S3, unofficial].
